title: Stine-Morrow (2007): True or False
instructions: Distinguish the two forms of engagement, study designs, limits on transfer, and the strength of the hypothesis. Use the article to choose True or False.

items.prompt: Mental mechanics involving rapid encoding and transformation of new information typically decline with age, whereas abilities based on knowledge and cultural acquisition can remain stable or increase.
items.explanation: The article describes cognitive aging as a multifaceted process involving both growth and decline. It contrasts the typical decline in fluid abilities with the potential stability or growth of crystallized abilities into late life.

items.prompt: Successful older readers may devote more attention to conceptual integration, chunk language input more frequently, and allocate more attention to situational features and discourse structures.
items.explanation: These adjustments can help accommodate age-related changes in processing capacity. More frequent chunking means pausing more often to integrate concepts.
items.source: Allocation adjustments in successful older readers

items.prompt: Attentional engagement and activity engagement both refer to the same process of selecting intellectually stimulating environments.
items.explanation: Attentional engagement concerns implementing task-specific processes through the allocation of cognitive effort. Activity engagement concerns habitually selecting intellectually stimulating environmental contexts.

items.prompt: In the SRLP model, text understanding depends on constructing mental representations at the levels of surface form, textbase, and situation model.
items.explanation: The model describes representations of the text's lexical expression, the ideas it conveys, and the situation suggested by those ideas. Component processes at these levels support language understanding and memory.
items.source: Levels of representation in the SRLP model

items.prompt: The negative feedback loop in the SRLP model stops processing at a given level when perceived comprehension falls below its reference value.
items.explanation: When the current representation is not good enough, the processor at that level demands more resources. The loop reduces the discrepancy until perceived comprehension satisfies the reference value.

items.prompt: Allocation policy is operationalized as the relative change in unit reading times as text-processing demands vary.
items.explanation: Regression coefficients relating reading times to text characteristics indicate a reader's allocation pattern. Examples include extra time for new concepts and for integration at clause or sentence boundaries; total reading time alone does not capture these adjustments.

items.prompt: In the study comparing accuracy and efficiency goals, older readers adjusted their reading-time allocation more strongly to the accuracy goal than younger readers did.
items.explanation: The observed pattern was the reverse: younger readers' time allocation was especially responsive to the accuracy goal. Older adults were less responsive, despite the expectation that reduced processing capacity would require them to allocate disproportionately more time for accurate recall.
items.source: Responsiveness to reading goals and Figure 2

items.prompt: Age differences in responsiveness to the accuracy goal were accounted for in part by working-memory capacity and memory self-efficacy.
items.explanation: The study linked responsiveness both to existing capacity and to beliefs that one could affect memory outcomes. The article therefore identifies self-efficacy, as well as capacity, as relevant to older adults' lower responsiveness to the goal.

items.prompt: The observation that people in intellectually challenging environments obtain higher cognitive scores establishes that activity engagement causally prevents cognitive decline.
items.explanation: People with greater inherent vitality may be more likely to seek out and sustain such activities. Engagement and cognitive outcomes may also correlate because they share an underlying cause, so the association does not establish the proposed causal effect.

items.prompt: Under the common-cause account discussed by the author, occupational engagement, leisure activities, and vulnerability to dementia may be biobehavioral markers of the same genetically driven aging process.
items.explanation: In this proposed account, the indicators can correlate because they derive from a common underlying process. Their association need not mean that one directly causes the others; the author presents this as a plausible alternative explanation.

items.prompt: The ACTIVE trial provided older adults with 10 sessions of training in memory, processing speed, or reasoning, and retention of training effects was demonstrated for up to 5 years.
items.explanation: This randomized clinical trial found training effects relative to a no-contact control group, with retention demonstrated for up to 5 years. The article emphasizes that the effects were highly specific to the abilities trained.

items.prompt: The effects of processing-speed training in ACTIVE transferred broadly to memory and reasoning.
items.explanation: The effects of processing-speed training were specific to speeded tasks. The article states that they did not transfer to memory or reasoning.

items.prompt: ACTIVE also objectively demonstrated transfer of training effects to everyday analogues of the trained abilities.
items.explanation: The article reports no demonstrated transfer to everyday analogues of the abilities. Its separate observation that reasoning trainees reported greater ease with instrumental activities of daily living is a self-report finding, not proof of that transfer.
items.source: Limits on transfer to everyday activities

items.prompt: Preliminary Senior Odyssey findings showed improved processing speed and relative increases in mindfulness and need for cognition compared with wait-list controls.
items.explanation: The preliminary findings also showed a marginal improvement in divergent thinking. The author explicitly notes that whether Senior Odyssey produces broad-based improvement in cognitive function remains to be seen.

items.prompt: The article establishes that individual choices have a greater causal influence on cognitive vitality than senescence does, confirming the Dumbledore hypothesis.
items.explanation: The hypothesis still requires empirical testing. The conclusion identifies interactions between attentional and activity engagement, conditions such as novelty, and psychosocial mechanisms such as self-efficacy and mindfulness as questions for further investigation.
items.source: Empirical status of the Dumbledore hypothesis
